title: How Fireplaces Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how fireplaces work, from the ancient hearth to the modern masonry fireplace. They cover the parts of a traditional fireplace (hearth, surround, firebox, throat, smoke chamber, smoke shelf, damper, spark arrestor, chimney cap, ash dump, glass doors), the physics of drafts, convection and radiation, negative pressure and neutral pressure planes, and why traditional fireplaces are inefficient (Ben Franklin's complaints). They discuss health and fire risks, wood selection and seasoning, starting a fire safely, efficiency upgrades like tubular grates and recirculators, wood stoves, gas log and gas fireplaces, ethanol and electric fireplaces, carbon monoxide safety, creosote and chimney fires, and the history of child chimney sweeps in England, including the Chimney Sweeps Acts and the 1875 death of George Brewster. The episode ends with listener mail from Colleen Zaker about grammar rules.

segments.title: Opening banter and live shows
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about recent live shows in Boston and Washington, D.C., then introduce the fireplace topic with notes on early controlled fire use and the history of the chimney.

segments.title: Fireplace history, inefficiency, and health concerns
segments.summary: They note that the fireplace design has changed little in about seven hundred years, that Ben Franklin complained about fireplace inefficiency, and that 77 percent of home buyers still want fireplaces. They discuss smoke-related respiratory risks and house fires.

segments.title: Anatomy of a fireplace
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck walk through the parts of a traditional fireplace: hearth, surround, firebox, throat, smoke chamber, smoke shelf, damper, spark arrestor, chimney cap, ash dump, and glass or screen doors.

segments.title: Physics of drafts, heat transfer, and smoke
segments.summary: They explain why fireplaces need air coming into the house, how heat rising creates draft, and the roles of conduction, convection, and radiation. They discuss negative pressure, why a fire can make a room colder, and how a fireplace draws far more room air than a wood stove.

segments.title: Wood stoves and modern stove designs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss wood stoves, their heat output and safety risks, their efficiency compared with open fireplaces, and mid-century and Swedish-style designs.

segments.title: Choosing and seasoning firewood and starting a fire
segments.summary: They cover hardwood versus softwood, seasoning wood for at least six months (ideally a year), testing with the hollow sound, grates and andirons, and safe fire starting with kindling and without accelerants.

segments.title: Neutral pressure plane and efficiency upgrades
segments.summary: They explain the neutral pressure plane and how opening a window can fix smoke backdrafting. They describe tubular grates, recirculating fans, and glass doors as ways to improve efficiency, and say open fireplaces lose more heat than they produce.

segments.title: Gas logs, gas fireplaces, ethanol and electric options
segments.summary: They discuss converting a wood fireplace to gas logs, the efficiency of sealed gas fireplaces, concerns about ventless gas units, ethanol fireplaces, and electric fireplaces, including the emissions tied to electricity generation.

segments.title: Fireplace safety, creosote, and chimney inspection
segments.summary: They cover carbon monoxide detectors, keeping flammable materials away, annual inspections, creosote buildup and chimney fires, the risks of chemical creosote logs, and advice to hire a chimney sweep.

segments.title: History of child chimney sweeps
segments.summary: They describe the use of child chimney sweeps in England, the soot trade, deaths from positional asphyxia and scrotal cancer, the Chimney Sweeps Acts of 1788 and 1840, and the 1875 death of George Brewster that led to enforcement.

segments.title: Listener mail: grammar police
segments.summary: Josh reads an email from Colleen Zaker, an English teacher, arguing that grammar rules are constantly evolving and that listeners should not be discouraged by grammar critics.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close with the show's contact information and a pointer to the How Stuff Works site for more on fireplaces.
